transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Jared Kim (HelioData SRE), Maya Singh (HelioData ML Infra), Omar Reyes (HelioData CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Customer seeing intermittent OOMs followed by timeouts in their private VPC deployment. Errors often surface under peak load with mixed batch sizes; sometimes CUDA driver logs show 'unknown error' and process restarts. Redwood suggests tracing nvprof, adjusting batch settings and KV cache eviction, and tuning retry backoff with idempotency keys.

00:00 Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we wanted to focus this deep dive on the OOMs and the CUDA timeouts you flagged, and then walk through retry semantics so we don't end up doubling work on retries.
00:18 Omar: yeah thanks Samir, from our side it's been a pretty rough week, we've had three incidents where the pod crashed, the model stopped responding, and then the customer facing requests timed out. we're running in our VPC with the private deployment — cpu + 8xA100 nodes, gpus pinned.
00:36 Lena: quick q — are you seeing the same model version across failures? quantization or fp16 enabled?
00:44 Maya: mostly the quantized 4-bit build we rolled out last month, and yes fp16 inference path enabled on a couple of endpoints. we thought quant helped but now suspect it's interacting badly with their custom kernels.
01:02 Samir: okay good, that aligns with what you reported in the ticket. can you paste the crash log lines?
01:10 Jared: sure i've got snippets — here's the typical line: "CUDA error: unspecified launch failure" followed by: "Segmentation fault (core dumped)" then the runtime restarts. sometimes dmesg shows an OOM killer entry, sometimes not.
01:28 Lena: that pattern usually means either memory corruption or a kernel timing out. if the kernel takes too long the CUDA watchdog on the driver can kill it — especially in environments with display drivers turned on. in headless datacenter you normally disable the watchdog but depending on the AMI/docker base it can still trigger.
01:52 Maya: hmm we are using the vanilla vendor AMI, we haven't tuned driver settings.
01:58 Samir: two angles to systematically check: first, memory pressure / KV cache bloat — if your KV cache isn't being pruned aggressively, long sequences or many concurrent requests can spike peak memory. second, kernel-level timeouts and mismatched libcudnn/cuBLAS versions which can cause rare crashes.
02:20 Lena: also batching heuristics — if a request suddenly arrives with a long context it can increase the peak token count in a batch; Redwood's runtime will batch by default, so under bursty traffic you can see big spikes.
02:36 Jared: yeah we see bursts where a single client sends long multi-turn histories. we expected KV cache to help but maybe it's the opposite if it keeps references alive.
02:46 Samir: exactly — KV cache reduces compute but holds onto memory. if you're pinning very long contexts with minimal eviction it raises resident set size. recommended: set a per-session KV TTL and a hard cap on per-worker KV memory.
03:02 Maya: does Redwood expose those knobs in the private deployment?
03:06 Lena: yes, in our 2025.10 runtime you can tune kv.max_entries_per_session and kv.global_memory_limit, plus eviction_policy. we'll share the config file.
03:18 Omar: what about retry behavior — sometimes the frontend retries with a 0 backoff and we end up replaying heavy requests which makes the spike worse.
03:28 Samir: that's a classic feedback loop. our retry semantics: we don't retry non-idempotent payloads by default; the client SDK does exponential backoff with jitter but only for 5xx/transport errors. in private deployments customers sometimes bypass SDK and have custom proxies which do aggressive sync retries.
03:52 Jared: so if a large request times out and the proxy retries immediately, that could double the simultaneous memory usage.
03:58 Lena: and worse if both attempts get batched together by the runtime — then you get a multiplied batch size. recommended pattern: idempotency keys and a short pre-retry check (e.g., 409 conflict on duplicate job id) or use a queuing layer to serialize heavy long-context calls.
04:18 Maya: okay makes sense. any guidance on safe batch sizes? our default was 16 concurrency with dynamic batching.
04:28 Lena: depends on model, sequence length distribution, and GPU type. rule of thumb: run a p99 memory profiler under representative load and derive a target 75% of observed peak as config. we often start with conservative batch_size 4-8 for long-context workloads, then increase as KV eviction is tuned.
04:46 Samir: also talk about quantization interactions — quant 4-bit can reduce memory but sometimes introduces extra kernel complexity that trips corner-case driver bugs. if you're seeing 'unspecified launch failure' mixed with quant builds, try a control test with non-quant FP16 to see if the failure rate changes.
05:02 Omar: we can run that; our prod is already quant but staging has FP16.
05:08 Jared: question — are there known cuBLAS/cuda driver versions that Redwood recommends? we recently updated drivers and that roughly coincides with these incidents.
05:16 Lena: yes we publish a compatibility matrix; current recommended stack for A100 is CUDA 12.x with cuBLAS/cuDNN matched to the runtime build. mismatches can cause silent corruption. we'll send the exact versions.
05:30 Maya: perfect. any quick mitigation if we need an immediate stop-gap during peak hours?
05:36 Samir: a few quick mitigations: 1) reduce auto-batching window so batches don't accumulate long-sequence requests; 2) scale up node count / reduce per-node batch target to spread memory; 3) temporarily fall back to a smaller model variant for bursty endpoints; 4) enable conservative KV eviction and free dormant sessions after N minutes.
05:56 Jared: about the fall back — how seamless is switching models in private deployment? we don't want weird state or session breakage.
06:06 Lena: runtime supports model variants and you can configure a fallback policy: canary then immediate fallback on OOM. sessions tied to a conversation id will need cache warmup again, but we can preserve session IDs and rehydrate states when moving back. it's not 0-downtime but it's fast.
06:28 Omar: are there any logs we should collect that's most helpful?
06:32 Lena: yes: 1) worker stderr/cuda-driver logs, 2) nvprof/cupti traces for the failing window, 3) runtime's per-process memory breakout and kv cache metrics, 4) the request payloads/timestamps if privacy allows.
06:46 Maya: we can share sanitized payloads. we'll need an internal ticket to extract nvprof traces.
06:52 Samir: on retries, we also recommend instrumenting request ids and returning 409 for duplicate job ids at the proxy level, or use an at-least-once queue with dedupe. that prevents duplicate heavy work.
07:12 Jared: does Redwood's runtime dedupe identical requests at the route level?
07:18 Lena: we have optional request-level dedupe and response cache for identical payloads — it's off by default because of cost, but for heavy, repeatable workloads it's helpful.
07:28 Omar: curious about pre-warm — how much does pre-warming reduce tail latencies and OOM risk?
07:34 Lena: pre-warm creates resident KV entries and preloads model weights so the first hot requests don't spike allocations. it reduces p95/p99 latency and evens memory usage. but it increases baseline memory, so you should balance with node count.
07:52 Maya: so for our traffic pattern, pre-warm during business hours and scale to zero at night?
07:58 Samir: yes that's a typical pattern. we also recommend scheduled padding — pre-warm a few workers before known campaign spikes.
08:08 Jared: we saw some "CUDA kernel hang" logs with stack traces pointing to a particular custom fused op in their graph. could that be a bad operator implementation?
08:18 Lena: yes fused or custom ops are common culprits. if you have custom kernels ensure they are compiled against the exact CUDA toolkit version and the runtime's expected compute capabilities. otherwise you can get undefined behavior.
08:30 Maya: we have a custom attention kernel. could that be causing memory corruption?
08:34 Lena: possibly. steps: reproduce locally with the same driver/runtime, run asan if possible, and run a single-worker stress with profiling. Redwood can help reproduce inside a private staging cluster we can spin up for you.
08:52 Omar: that would be great. what's the turnaround on spinning that staging cluster?
08:56 Samir: typically 24-48 hours for a private VPC staging spin-up once we have the account details and some baseline config.
09:04 Jared: earlier you mentioned retry semantics with respect to idempotency. do you have recommended header patterns?
09:10 Lena: common pattern: X-Idempotency-Key or idempotency-key header; use UUID per logical request from client; proxy checks dedupe cache for N minutes. Redwood SDKs provide idempotency helpers.
09:26 Maya: one more item — for timeouts we're seeing the HTTP front-end time out at 30s and then the orchestration retries. could increasing request timeout help?
09:34 Samir: possibly, but increasing client timeout just ties up connections longer. better to fix root cause (reduce peak mem) and add backoff on retries. If you must, bump to 60s and add server-side cancellation hooks so long-running requests can be aborted if the worker is overloaded.
09:56 Jared: is there a recommended backoff config? our current proxy uses immediate then 3 retries every 1s.
10:02 Lena: we recommend exponential backoff with jitter: initial 200-500ms, double each try, cap ~5-10s, and max 3-4 retries. for heavy requests consider 1-2 retries max.
10:16 Maya: related question: does Redwood's retry on internal transient errors ever replay partial KV cache states and cause duplication?
10:24 Lena: our runtime's retry is at request boundary — retries spawn a new request; KV state is per-session and persisted only if explicitly checkpointed. partial writes during a failed request won't be committed to durable storage unless configured. so you generally won't get half-committed KV from retries unless you use an explicit transactional layer.
10:44 Omar: ok that reduces a class of worries.
10:48 Samir: i want to propose an experiment: step one, reproduce crash in staging with identical driver; step two, run with FP16 non-quant; step three, toggle kv eviction/hard caps and watch p99 mem; step four, test proxy retry policy with injected timeouts. agreed?
11:06 Maya: agreed. we'll schedule the staging window.
11:10 Jared: what about preemptible GPU behavior in our cluster — we use spot-like nodes sometimes; does that affect times where we see OOM?
11:18 Lena: preemptions can cause sudden evictions and restart storms; when combined with aggressive retries it looks like an OOM spike. having graceful draining and slower retry backoff helps.
11:30 Omar: any immediate config change you'd recommend we flip tonight?
11:34 Samir: flip KV eviction to LRU with a low threshold, reduce batching window to 25ms, and set client-side backoff to exponential. that should reduce immediate risk.
11:54 Maya: we can do those tonight.
11:58 Lena: i'll send the exact config diffs after the call.
12:02 Samir: good — i also want to touch on observability: set up longer retention on the GPU metrics and CUDA driver logs for at least 7 days so we can correlate.
12:16 Jared: we currently keep only 48 hours, will extend.
12:20 Omar: any red flags about running A100 with quant-4 builds in private?
12:26 Lena: none inherent, but quantized kernels sometimes use custom fused ops that are less battle-tested. when we onboarded a customer before they found a driver / kernel mismatch that only surfaced under sustained long sequences. so the usual guidance holds: validate in staging under stress and have a quick rollback path.
12:44 Maya: are there telemetry hooks we can add to detect memory creeping before crash? like an early warning?
12:50 Lena: yes set thresholds and alerts on worker.rss and kv.memory_usage; also alert on rising queue latency and rising batch sizes. a gradual rise across those metrics is a good early warning.
13:06 Samir: ok i'll summarize next steps at the end and drop the docs. any other questions?
13:10 Omar: not right now.
13:12 -- midcall debugging --
22:05 (interrupted) Jared: i uploaded the crash snippet to the shared drive — filename: heliod_cuda_crash_20260510.log
22:22 Lena: got it, i'm taking a look now, quick eye — i see traces showing a custom op invocation right before the unspecified launch failure. can you also attach the nvprof slice for 2026-05-10T03:14?
22:40 Jared: uploading now.
23:10 Maya: one more note: our ops team changed the kernel driver last week, maybe that's the trigger.
23:20 Lena: driver change is a likely suspect. please provide kernel/driver versions and build IDs.
24:05 Samir: re retry semantics — we'll send the written doc and a recommended proxy config that uses idempotency keys, exponential backoff and a duplicate-detect endpoint behavior for heavy jobs.
24:20 Omar: great.
30:02 Lena: wanted to unpack the CUDA timeout case — sometimes the driver returns a TDR (timeout detection and recovery) if a kernel runs longer than the driver's threshold. On clouds this is muted but on certain VPC images the TDR is active. disabling TDR or using the compute only mode can help.
30:26 Jared: how safe is disabling TDR?
30:30 Lena: in dedicated compute clusters it's safe; on shared servers it's not. since you're on private dedicated nodes, it's an acceptable mitigation with the caveat you won't get automatic GPU reset on hung kernels.
30:44 Maya: we'll review with ops.
30:48 Samir: another thing: implement a graceful request size cap — refuse requests over N tokens with a clear 413-like response so clients can't accidentally submit huge contexts.
31:02 Jared: yes we actually had a client sending large context dumps — we'll implement that.
31:08 Omar: can Redwood implement the 413 behavior at the route config?
31:12 Lena: yes it's a configurable router policy. we'll add an example.
31:22 -- last 15 minutes focused on runbook and next steps --
40:03 Samir: quick runbook sketch: detect rising worker.rss -> throttle new sessions -> drop long non-idempotent requests with 413 -> increase retry backoff -> if OOM persists, trigger fallback to smaller model -> notify on-call and open postmortem.
40:28 Maya: pretty actionable.
40:34 Jared: timeline on docs?
40:38 Samir: i'll send the retry semantics doc and the staging spin-up checklist by 2026-05-14. Lena will send config diffs and the compatibility matrix.
40:52 Lena: yes sending both today/tomorrow.
